The evidence is moderate due to the limited sample size and early termination of the study.

analysis.research_and_practice_implications: DBS-based HBsAg testing is recommended for community screening, primary care, and resource-limited settings due to its high diagnostic accuracy. The review emphasizes the need for standardization of DBS protocols to enhance reliability and consistency. Overall, the findings suggest that DBS testing can be a valuable tool for HBV diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited areas.

title: Candidate epistatic mutation clusters in occult hepatitis B virus genotype D: a critical narrative review of the evidence gap and a proposed testable framework

analysis.scope_and_question: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) genotype D is the dominant genotype across the Middle East. The review focuses on the role of epistatic mutation clusters in occult hepatitis B infection (OBI) and the need for a testable framework to investigate their impact on HBsAg detectability, secretion, or replication in genotype D.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review critically appraises the available evidence, distinguishing established findings from extrapolation and hypothesis using an explicit grading scheme. It proposes a four-level evidence hierarchy to evaluate mutation clusters, including co-occurrence, phylogenetically corrected covariation, experimental single-versus-combination comparison, and mechanistic validation. The review also outlines the sequencing, functional, structural, and clinical studies required to test the hypothesis directly.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Published data on HBsAg mutation clusters in genotype D reach Level 1–2 at most. The decisive Level 3 experiment, site-directed reconstruction of candidate clusters versus their constituent single mutants on a defined genotype D backbone, has not been performed. Epistasis is a biologically plausible, under-tested mechanism that may help explain why single mutations incompletely account for OBI.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: It is not yet established whether combinations of co-occurring surface mutations interact non-additively, that is epistatically, to influence HBsAg detectability, secretion, or replication in genotype D. Genotype-D-specific and Middle-East-specific datasets adequate for cluster-level analysis are limited. Direct evidence linking coinfection to selection of mutation clusters is absent. Structural inference remains constrained because recent cryo-EM structures of HBsAg subviral particles do not resolve the ‘a’ determinant loops at the resolution required to interpret mutation-cluster-level conformational perturbations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The functional and structural data required to answer these questions are largely absent. The review proposes and applies a four-level evidence hierarchy to determine whether candidate epistatic clusters contribute to OBI in genotype D. It should not be presented as an established driver.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of epistatic mutation clusters in occult hepatitis B infection (OBI) in HBV genotype D, which is dominant in the Middle East. It highlights the limitations of current evidence, noting that while individual surface-protein escape mutations are well characterised, they do not fully account for OBI. The review proposes a four-level evidence hierarchy to assess the impact of mutation clusters on HBsAg detectability, secretion, or replication. It identifies the need for experimental single-versus-combination comparisons and mechanistic validation, which have not yet been conducted. The review also underscores the lack of genotype-D-specific and Middle-East-specific datasets, as well as the absence of direct evidence linking coinfection to mutation cluster selection. Finally, it calls for further research to address these gaps and test the hypothesis that epistasis may explain the incomplete understanding of OBI in genotype D.

title: Seroprevalence update of Hepatitis B Virus, Hepatitis C Virus, and human immunodeficiency virus among people who inject drugs in Kuwait: a cross-sectional study at a national addiction treatment center

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to update the seroprevalence of Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), Hepatitis C Virus (HCV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) among people who inject drugs (PWID) in Kuwait, as PWID represent a key population disproportionately affected by blood-borne viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional study was conducted from January to December 2024 at Kuwait’s national addiction treatment center, enrolling 1,287 consecutive patients. The cohort was predominantly male (86.6%) and Kuwaiti (87.3%), with a median age of 33 years.
analysis.methods: Serological screening for HBsAg, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV was performed using chemiluminescent immunoassays. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with each infection, except for HBV due to the extremely low number of HBV-reactive cases (n = 2).

Female sex was associated with significantly lower odds of HIV infection (aOR = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.02–0.92, p = 0.04).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study reveals a concerning increase in HIV prevalence and a shift to universal active HCV viremia among PWID in Kuwait compared to 2017 data. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings underscore an urgent need for the scale-up of targeted harm reduction, test-and-treat strategies, and integrated care services to curb transmission among PWID in Kuwait.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The extremely low number of HBV-reactive cases (n = 2) limits the ability to derive adjusted estimates for HBV. The evidence is moderate due to the cross-sectional design and potential for confounding factors.

title: On‐Treatment Reassessment of Type IV Collagen 7S and M2BPGi‐Qt Improves Long‐Term Hepatocellular Carcinoma Risk Stratification in Chronic Hepatitis B

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major complication in patients with chronic hepatitis B receiving nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy despite effective viral suppression. The study was conducted over a median follow-up period of 12.6 years, with serum 4COL7S and M2BPGi‐Qt measured at baseline and 1 year after treatment initiation.
analysis.methods: Serum 4COL7S and M2BPGi‐Qt were measured at baseline and 1 year after treatment initiation. Landmark, Kaplan–Meier, and multivariable Cox analyses were performed to evaluate the association between these markers and HCC development.
analysis.main_results: During a median follow-up of 12.6 years, 45 patients (14.1%) developed HCC. In multivariable analyses, 1-year 4COL7S remained independently associated with subsequent HCC development after adjustment for baseline mPAGE-B, 1-year HBsAg-HQ, and 1-year HBcrAg (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.167; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.001–1.344; p = 0.042). M2BPGi‐Qt showed consistent supportive findings (adjusted HR, 1.272; 95% CI, 1.101–1.468; p = 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: On-treatment 4COL7S was independently associated with subsequent HCC development and may serve as a novel direct fibrosis marker for long-term risk stratification in NA-treated chronic hepatitis B. M2BPGi‐Qt provided supportive prognostic information.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that reassessing on-treatment 4COL7S and M2BPGi‐Qt can improve long-term risk stratification for hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with chronic hepatitis B undergoing nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a retrospective cohort study, which may introduce bias and limit the strength of causal inference. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether on-treatment assessment of type IV collagen 7S (4COL7S) and M2BPGi‐Qt could improve long-term hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk stratification in patients with chronic hepatitis B receiving nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy. A retrospective cohort of 319 patients was followed for a median of 12.6 years, with serum markers measured at baseline and 1 year post-treatment. The primary endpoint was HCC development, and multivariable Cox analyses were used to assess associations. Results showed that elevated 1-year levels of both markers were significantly associated with increased HCC risk, with 4COL7S independently linked to HCC development after adjustment for other factors. The authors concluded that 4COL7S may serve as a novel direct fibrosis marker for long-term risk stratification, while M2BPGi‐Qt provided supportive prognostic information. analysis.methods: Quantitative analysis was performed using SPSS. Qualitative themes were synthesised via a hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis, using QCAmap.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a nomogram to predict 5-year mortality in patients with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis complicated by portal vein thrombosis (PVT) using a training cohort of 961 patients. The authors propose the nomogram as a clinically useful tool for individualized risk stratification in this high-risk subgroup.

analysis.methods: Consecutive adult participants with chronic hepatitis B (PWHB) alone or HBV/HIV coinfection underwent PUSH with operators blinded to clinical data, and accuracy was evaluated using transient elastography (TE) as the reference standard for fibrosis and cirrhosis and comprehensive abdominal ultrasound by an experienced radiographer for liver lesions.

title: Hepatitis B Immunization Among Healthcare Students: A Narrative Review of Occupational Risk, Seroprotection, and Immunization Management

analysis.scope_and_question: Healthcare students face an occupational risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) exposure during clinical training, often many years after receiving their primary vaccination series in infancy or childhood.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A narrative review was conducted through a systematic literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus, covering publications from January 2000 to December 2025, supplemented by key seminal references. After the removal of duplicates and stepwise screening, 49 references were selected for final inclusion.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Pooled seroprotection prevalence at clinical training entry is approximately 73.8% (95% CI 69.1–78.0%), with substantially lower rates among students vaccinated in infancy—as low as 28% at 16–20 years post-vaccination in longitudinal data—compared with adolescence immunization. The majority of students with non-protective titres retain immunological memory, with 90.9% (95% CI 87.7–93.3%) demonstrating an anamnestic response after a single booster dose. Post-exposure prophylaxis pathways depend critically on pre-existing immunological status, reinforcing the operational value of pre-clinical serological screening.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Progressive waning of anti-hepatitis B surface (anti-HBs) antibody titres, heterogeneous vaccination histories in international student cohorts, high rates of underreported needlestick injuries, and variable occupational health protocols across institutions raise important questions about the adequacy of pre-clinical immunization surveillance in this population. International student cohorts present additional complexity due to heterogeneous vaccination schedules, documentation gaps, and variable natural immunity profiles.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Systematic pre-clinical serological screening (anti-HBs, HBsAg, and anti-HBc), combined with evidence-based stepwise immunization management and structured educational interventions, is essential to protect healthcare students from occupational HBV exposure. The primary operational goal of screening is the identification of the approximately 5% of true non-responders who require tailored occupational health management.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines hepatitis B virus (HBV) immunization among healthcare students, focusing on occupational exposure risk, seroprotection, and immunization management. It highlights the progressive waning of anti-HBs antibody titres, heterogeneous vaccination histories, and underreporting of needlestick injuries as critical challenges. The pooled seroprotection prevalence at clinical training entry is approximately 73.8%, with lower rates among students vaccinated in infancy. Most students with non-protective titres retain immunological memory, and post-exposure prophylaxis depends on pre-existing immunity. The review emphasizes the need for systematic pre-clinical serological screening and tailored occupational health management to align with WHO 2030 viral hepatitis-elimination targets.
